construction_notes: Home value HV_it is built in Equation (1) as the public valuation times the owned share, scaled by the mean ratio of sales price to public valuation among the K homes sold in the same year/municipality/housing type/valuation quartile cluster, summed over the woman and her partner.
Each woman is assigned the HV of the first house she is seen to purchase, regardless of whether she subsequently moves.

Public valuations occur in January of the prior year until the end of 2003 and in October of the prior year afterwards; privately owned properties are valued in uneven years and adjusted in even years.

All monetary variables are in 100,000 Danish Kroner deflated to 2006 prices with the consumer price index; the 2006 exchange rate was approximately 0.17 USD per DKK, or 0.12 adjusting for purchasing power parity, and the PPP rate is used for international comparisons.
The number of inpatient days excludes the admission related to the childbirth and the following four days.
The once-lagged one-year change independent variable implies an age range of 20 to 44 for the fertility analysis.
Income quartiles are defined over the full sample period (footnote 27).
Predicted outcomes in Table 2 and Table 7 come from the main specification estimated without the lagged one-year home value change or fixed effects.
Multiple births are excluded from the infant health analysis, and observations with missing birth weight are dropped for the birth weight outcomes.
Danish household consumption is imputed from income and year-to-year wealth changes using the method of Browning and Leth-Peterson (2003), since the register data contain no consumption measure.

links.pointer_quote: Our findings suggest that there is a positive effect of home price increases on fertility: a 100,000 DK (approximately $12,000 in 2006, adjusting for purchasing power parity) increase in home prices in the prior year increases the likelihood of giving birth by 0.27 percentage points, or 2.32% relative to the mean.
They find an effect of 2.11% for each $12,000 of home price increase, which is very close to the 2.32% effect we document in Denmark.

claims.statement: A 100,000 DKK increase in the lagged one-year home value raises the probability that a homeowner woman gives birth by 0.27 percentage points (2.32% of the mean).

treatment.label: Lagged one-year home value change (100,000 DKK)

register_source.value: The State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public valuations, sales prices, ownership, housing type)

definition.value: Once-lagged one-year change in the estimated value of the first home the woman (or her partner) purchased: dHV_{i,t-1} = HV_{i,t-1} - HV_{i,t-2}, in 100,000 DKK deflated to 2006 prices with the CPI. HV is built in Equation (1) as the public valuation times the owned share, scaled by the mean sale-price-to-public-valuation ratio among homes actually sold in the same year/municipality/housing type/valuation-quartile cluster. Each woman keeps the value of the first house she is seen to purchase even if she later moves.

units.value: probability of giving birth in a year (0/1) per 100,000 DKK increase in home value

magnitude.interpretation: % Effect = 2.32 (the effect of a 100,000 DKK change in home prices relative to the mean fertility rate); 100,000 DKK is approximately $12,000 at purchasing power parity. R2 = 0.060. The paper notes the standard deviation of one-year lagged home price growth is about 1, so this is also roughly the effect of a one standard deviation increase.

estimand.target_population: Danish women aged 20-44 who first became home owners between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42, i.e. homeowner families experiencing short-run home price variation
estimand.time_horizon: birth in year t, one year after the measured one-year home value change (t-2 to t-1)

population.description: Danish women aged 20 to 44 who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18 to 42
subgroups_defined: family income quartile (defined over the full sample period)
population.selection: Women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who became a homeowner between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18 to 42, after house-level screens (residential use, clusters with at least five sales, normal sales between individuals, non-negative valuation and sales price, single address, sales price between 40% and 300% of public valuation) and woman-level screens (complete data on household income, home price and home ownership; partner did not purchase before the couple formed; public valuation changed by less than 50% year on year; not in the 1st or 99th percentile of the lagged one-year price change).

identification.source_of_variation: Short-run (one-year) variation in the estimated market value of the first home the woman or her partner purchased, used within municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase cells; the period spans the Danish housing boom of the early- to mid-2000s. The paper describes the design as the reduced form of using first-home price changes as an instrument for the price changes actually experienced.

key_assumptions.assumption: Changes in home prices are unrelated to unobserved characteristics that also correlate with the likelihood of giving birth and with birth outcomes (conditional ignorability given the controls and fixed effects).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 shows average observable characteristics and thirteen predicted outcomes by quartile of the lagged one-year home price change; the paper reports no discernible pattern across quartiles.

heterogeneity.finding: Effects are quite stable across age groups for those below 40; the least responsive group in percent terms is 25-29 (1.47%), the most responsive 35-39 (2.89%); the effect declines substantially above 40 and is not statistically significant for 20-24 or 40-44 year olds (Table 5, Panel A).
Largest for first-time mothers (0.0056, 3.65%); statistically significant for 1 and 2 existing children; not significant for 3+ children, though the percent effect is over 3% (Table 5, Panel B).
Women in the middle of the income distribution are most responsive; the bottom-quartile estimate is not statistically significant (Table 5, Panel C).
Little evidence of heterogeneity by completed education; the effects are similarly sized and statistically significant in all four groups (Table 5, Panel D).
Effects of increases (0.0038) and decreases (-0.0040) are roughly equal and opposite, suggesting symmetry.

value.claimed_domain: The authors read the Danish estimate as evidence about homeowner households generally: because the per-dollar response is virtually identical to the US, they argue that Denmark's pro-natalist policies do not mitigate housing wealth effects on fertility and that US and Danish households have similar preferences for children.
boundary_conditions: homeowner households, which the paper argues are not credit constrained
real wealth changes converted at purchasing power parity
short-run home price changes rather than price levels

theory_referenced: household utility maximization framework with children and child health as normal goods
credit constraints and the net price of children

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Put on a monetary scale, our results are in line with those found in previous studies and virtually identical to that of Lovenheim and Mumford (2013), who use data from a similar period.
Estimates from a similar model in Australia using micro data from 2001-2014 show a fertility effect of 1.36% per $12,000 (Atalay, Li, and Whelan 2017)
results from Japan during the housing market downturn of the early 1990s indicates a fertility effect of 2.8% per $12,000 among those with home loans
Using city-by-year aggregate data for the period 1990 to 2007, Dettling and Kearney (2014) find an effect of 6.0% per $12,000 of home price increase.

population.description: Danish women aged 20 to 44 who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who first purchased a home between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18 to 42, conditional on giving birth; multiple births excluded, restricted to mothers aged 20-24

population.selection: Women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who became a homeowner between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18 to 42, after house-level screens (residential use, clusters with at least five sales, normal sales between individuals, non-negative valuation and sales price, single address, sales price between 40% and 300% of public valuation) and woman-level screens (complete data on household income, home price and home ownership; partner did not purchase before the couple formed; public valuation changed by less than 50% year on year; not in the 1st or 99th percentile of the lagged one-year price change). Infant health estimates are additionally conditional on giving birth, with multiple births excluded and (for birth weight outcomes) missing birth weight dropped.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on becoming a first-time home owner: women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who became a homeowner between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18 to 42.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A-1 Panel B reports the observations dropped at each screen; the paper notes that homeowners have a higher fertility rate than the population because of selection into home ownership.

key_assumptions.assumption: Every woman is assigned the price changes of her first purchased home even if she moves, which the paper describes as the reduced form of using first-home price changes as an instrument for the price changes actually experienced; the assigned change is assumed to affect outcomes only through the home price variation it proxies.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues this makes the estimates less sensitive to bias from endogenous parent mobility than prior work, and notes that mobility rates are low in Denmark.

implies_edges.from: first-home price change assigned after moving

key_assumptions.assumption: Bias would remain only if higher fertility households, or those with better underlying infant health, were better at predicting future home price growth when they purchase a home, in a way uncorrelated with the observables, the age at purchase and the year of purchase.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text as the residual threat after the municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects are included; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Infant health estimates are conditional on giving birth, so the sample of births is itself affected by the treatment; home price changes can shift infant health both by changing the composition of births and by changing outcomes among inframarginal births.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 7 regresses the characteristics of mothers who give birth on the lagged home price change and finds compositional shifts; the paper reports that mother fixed effects models give positive but economically small effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: Every woman is assigned the price changes of her first purchased home even if she moves, which the paper describes as the reduced form of using first-home price changes as an instrument for the price changes actually experienced; the assigned change is assumed to affect outcomes only through the home price variation it proxies.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues this makes the estimates less sensitive to bias from endogenous parent mobility than prior work, and notes that mobility rates are low in Denmark.

key_assumptions.assumption: Bias would remain only if higher fertility households, or those with better underlying infant health, were better at predicting future home price growth when they purchase a home, in a way uncorrelated with the observables, the age at purchase and the year of purchase.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text as the residual threat after the municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects are included; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on becoming a first-time home owner: women who were not home owners at the beginning of 1992-1993 and who became a homeowner between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18 to 42.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A-1 Panel B reports the observations dropped at each screen; the paper notes that homeowners have a higher fertility rate than the population because of selection into home ownership.

key_assumptions.assumption: Every woman is assigned the price changes of her first purchased home even if she moves, which the paper describes as the reduced form of using first-home price changes as an instrument for the price changes actually experienced; the assigned change is assumed to affect outcomes only through the home price variation it proxies.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues this makes the estimates less sensitive to bias from endogenous parent mobility than prior work, and notes that mobility rates are low in Denmark.

implies_edges.from: first-home price change assigned after moving

key_assumptions.assumption: Bias would remain only if higher fertility households, or those with better underlying infant health, were better at predicting future home price growth when they purchase a home, in a way uncorrelated with the observables, the age at purchase and the year of purchase.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text as the residual threat after the municipality-by-year and age-of-purchase-by-year-of-purchase fixed effects are included; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Infant health estimates are conditional on giving birth, so the sample of births is itself affected by the treatment; home price changes can shift infant health both by changing the composition of births and by changing outcomes among inframarginal births.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 7 regresses the characteristics of mothers who give birth on the lagged home price change and finds compositional shifts; the paper reports that mother fixed effects models give positive but economically small effects.
